Find the numbers $x, y, z$ satisfying all of the following $3$ equations.
$$\begin{cases} y + z = 3 \\ x + z = 5 \\ x + y = 4 \end{cases}$$

Two points $P, Q$ are taken on the side $BC$ of a parallelogram $ABCD$ so that
$$BP : PQ : QC = 3 : 2 : \sqrt{7}.$$
Let $R$ be the intersection of the lines $AP$ and $CD$, and $S$ the intersection of the lines $AQ$ and $CD$. Find the value of $\dfrac{DS}{SR}$.

How many integers between $1$ and $2003$ inclusive have an even number of positive divisors?
For example, the positive divisors of $6$ are the $4$ numbers $1, 2, 3, 6$, so $6$ satisfies this condition.

A point $D$ is taken inside an isosceles triangle $ABC$ with $AB = AC = 5$, $BC = 6$; let $E, F$ be the intersection points, other than $A$, of the circle with diameter $AD$ with the sides $AB, AC$ respectively. If $DE = 1$ and $DF = 2$, find the area of triangle $DBC$.
There is a right triangle all of whose side lengths are integers. If one of its sides has length $18$, find all possible values of the perimeter of this triangle.
There is a quadrilateral $ABCD$ with $AB = 3$, $BC = 4$, $CD = 5$, $DA = 6$, and the angle between the lines $AC$ and $BD$ is $45^\circ$. Find the area of this quadrilateral.

The positive integers $a, b, c, d$ satisfy both of the following equations.
$$\begin{cases} a + b = cd \\ c + d = ab \end{cases}$$
How many such quadruples $(a, b, c, d)$ are there?

There is a regular tetrahedron $ABCD$ with edge length $1$; let $O$ be the centre of the sphere passing through its $4$ vertices. The tetrahedron is cut successively by the following $3$ planes.
• the plane through $O$ parallel to the $2$ lines $BC$, $AD$
• the plane through $O$ parallel to the $2$ lines $CA$, $BD$
• the plane through $O$ parallel to the $2$ lines $AB$, $CD$
The tetrahedron is then divided into several solids. Find the volume of the solid containing the point $A$.

Consider the operation of applying to a pair of numbers $(x, y)$, each at least $1$, one of the following operations Ⓐ, Ⓑ.
Ⓐ Choose a number $a$ with $\frac{1}{x} \leq a \leq y$, multiply $x$ by $a$ and multiply $y$ by $\frac{1}{a}$. That is, replace $(x, y)$ by $\left(ax, \frac{y}{a}\right)$.
Ⓑ Add $1$ to both $x$ and $y$. That is, replace $(x, y)$ by $(x+1, y+1)$.
These operations are applied repeatedly starting from $(1, 1)$. For example, applying Ⓑ first gives $(2, 2)$; then applying Ⓐ with $a = \frac{3}{2}$ gives $\left(3, \frac{4}{3}\right)$; applying Ⓑ $3$ times to this gives $\left(6, \frac{13}{3}\right)$; and further applying Ⓐ with $a = \frac{1}{3}$ gives $(2, 13)$.
Among the pairs of positive integers that can never be obtained from $(1, 1)$ by applying the operations repeatedly in this way, find those for which the sum of the two numbers is largest.
$15$ people played a round-robin chess tournament, and there were no $2$ people whose numbers of wins, losses and draws were respectively equal. Find the largest possible total number of drawn games.

Find the value of
$$103 \times 103 - 97 \times 97.$$
$ABC$ is a right triangle with $\angle A = 90^\circ$. If $\angle B$ is $48^\circ$ larger than $\angle C$, find $\angle B$.

In the plane there is a regular hexagon with side length $1$. Let $S$ be the area of the part lying outside the regular hexagon of the set of points whose distance from at least one vertex of the regular hexagon is at most $1$. Let $T$ be the area of a regular hexagon with side length $1$. Find $S - T$.
Here the ratio of the circumference of a circle to its diameter is $\pi$.

$m, n$ are positive integers satisfying the following conditions.
$$\begin{cases} 3m - 1 = n \\ (n - 7)m = 16 \end{cases}$$
Find $n$.

Solve the following cryptarithm and write the number corresponding to IMO.
$$\begin{array}{r} I\,M\,O \\ \& \\ J\,M\,O \\ +\quad \& \\ \hline J\,J\,M\,O \end{array}$$
Here, solving a cryptarithm means determining a correspondence between letters and digits such that the above equality holds, according to the following conditions.
• Each of $I, M, O, \&, J$ corresponds to one of the digits $0, 1, 2, \ldots, 9$; the same letter corresponds to the same digit and different letters to different digits. That is, IMO is the $3$-digit number formed by writing the digit corresponding to $I$, the digit corresponding to $M$ and the digit corresponding to $O$ in this order.
• The leading letters $I$, $\&$, $J$ do not correspond to $0$.
• The digit corresponding to $I$ is not necessarily $1$. Also, the digit corresponding to $O$ is not necessarily $0$.

There is a wizard who can use magic A and magic B. Using magic A, every strawberry present changes simultaneously into $1$ strawberry and $1$ banana; using magic B, every banana present changes simultaneously into $1$ strawberry and $1$ banana. Starting from a state with $1$ strawberry and $1$ banana, how many times in total must magic be used, using magics A and B some number of times, to reach a state with $15$ strawberries and $877$ bananas?

Among the ways of arranging a total of $8$ balls of the $3$ colours red, blue and yellow in a row, how many use an odd number of red balls? Here there are enough balls of each colour, and some colour may be unused.
There is a triangle $ABC$ with $BC = 3$, $CA = 2$, $AB = 4$. Two points $D, E$ are taken on the side $AB$ so that $AD = 1$ and $\angle ACD = \angle BCE$. Find the length of the segment $BE$.

There are $7$ politicians and some factions. A faction is a set to which one or more politicians belong. For any $2$ factions, if there is a politician belonging to both, then one of them always contains the other. Find the largest possible number of factions.
Here a set consisting of a single person, and the set consisting of all $7$ people, are also factions.

In a quadrilateral $ABCD$, the segments $AC$ and $BD$ meet at the point $P$. Moreover,
$$AB = BP = AD, \qquad \angle ABC = \angle BDC, \qquad \angle BCD = \angle CAD$$
hold. Find $\angle BCD$.

For non-negative integers $a, b$, denote by $a * b$ the remainder when $a \times b$ is divided by $10$. Consider the operation that makes, from a triple $(a, b, c)$ of $3$ integers each between $0$ and $9$ inclusive, the triple $(a * b, b * c, c * a)$ of $3$ integers between $0$ and $9$ inclusive. Here triples that differ only in order, such as $(2, 7, 0)$ and $(2, 0, 7)$, are regarded as different.
For example, $(6, 5, 0)$ can be made from $(2, 3, 5)$.
How many triples in total can be made by performing this operation once?
$2^{2004}$ is divided by each of $1, 2, 3, \ldots, 2^{2004}$, and the quotient and remainder are found. How many different integers occur as quotients?
Find all positive integers that leave remainder $11$ both when dividing $197$ and when dividing $290$.
In a triangle $OAB$ of area $6$, let $P, Q$ be the midpoints of the sides $OA, OB$ respectively, and let $G$ be the intersection of $PB$ and $QA$. Find the area of the quadrilateral $OPGQ$.
The real numbers $x, y, z$ satisfy $2x + 3y - z = 9$ and $5x + 4y - 3z = 20$. Find the value of $9x - 4y - 7z$.

The number written as $110$ in the decimal system is written as $420$ in base five, again with $3$ digits. How many positive integers in all have the same number of digits in the decimal system and in base five?

For example, joining the $3$ circled points in the lower left figure gives a triangle, but choosing $3$ points lying on a straight line, as in the lower right figure, does not give a triangle.

The product of the $3$ numbers in every column and the product of the $3$ numbers in every row are both $2005$.

$$\frac{108}{1}, \frac{107}{2}, \frac{106}{3}, \ldots, \frac{3}{106}, \frac{2}{107}, \frac{1}{108},$$
find the one closest to $1$.
Here closest to $1$ means that the absolute value of the difference from $1$ is smallest.

There is an $8 \times 8$ grid. Coins are placed face up or face down on some of the cells so that the following conditions hold.
• If there is a face-up coin on a cell, there is no other coin in the same row.
• If there is a face-down coin on a cell, there is no other coin in the same column.
At most how many coins can be placed?

For any triangle, its $3$ medians (the lines joining a vertex to the midpoint of the opposite side) meet at one point. This point is called the centroid of the triangle.
Now, joining by edges the centroids of adjacent faces of a regular octahedron gives a cube. How many times the volume of the original regular octahedron is the volume of the cube obtained in this way?

There are $2$ cards, a red one and a blue one, with each of $1, 2, \ldots, 10$ written on it. When $3$ cards are chosen from these $20$ cards, in how many ways can they be chosen so that the sum of the numbers written on them is at most $16$?

Among the sets of $3$ distinct positive integers such that the sum of any $2$ of them is a perfect square, find all those for which the sum of the $3$ numbers is smallest. Here sets that differ only in order, such as "$1$, $2$ and $3$" and "$3$, $2$ and $1$", are regarded as the same.

$x, y, z$ are pairwise distinct $2$-digit positive integers; the units digit of $x$ equals the tens digit of $y$, the units digit of $y$ equals the tens digit of $z$, and the units digit of $z$ equals the tens digit of $x$. How many values are possible for the greatest common divisor of such $3$ numbers $x, y, z$?

Consider the following equation.
$$x^2 + xy + y^2 + 3x + 6y + 6 = 0 \qquad (*)$$
(1) Find all pairs of integers $x, y$ satisfying equation $(*)$ with $x = 1$.
(2) Find all pairs of integers $x, y$ satisfying equation $(*)$.

(1) We want to paint each cell of a $3 \times 3$ grid with one of the colours red, blue, yellow. Adjacent cells must not be painted with the same colour; some colour may be unused. In how many ways can this be done? Here paintings that coincide after rotation or reflection are counted as different.
(2) In (1), what is the answer when the colours available are the $4$ colours red, blue, yellow, green?

Let $m, n$ be integers with $m, n \geq 2$. We want to write an integer in each cell of a grid with $m$ rows and $n$ columns so that the following conditions hold.
(i) There is at least $1$ cell in which a non-zero integer is written.
(ii) For each cell $S$, the sum $t(S)$ of the integers written in all the cells adjacent to $S$ is $0$.
For example, let $m = 3$, $n = 4$ and suppose $1$ is written in every cell:
$$\begin{array}{|c|c|c|c|} \hline 1 & 1 & 1 & 1 \\ \hline 1 & 1 & 1 & 1 \\ \hline 1 & 1 & 1 & 1 \\ \hline \end{array}$$
Then showing $t(S)$ in each cell $S$ gives the following.
$$\begin{array}{|c|c|c|c|} \hline 2 & 3 & 3 & 2 \\ \hline 3 & 4 & 4 & 3 \\ \hline 2 & 3 & 3 & 2 \\ \hline \end{array}$$
Hence writing the integers in this way does not satisfy condition (ii).
When integers can be written so as to satisfy the $2$ conditions, $(m, n)$ is called a good pair. For example, consider the pair $(2, 2)$.
$$\begin{array}{|c|c|} \hline 0 & 1 \\ \hline -1 & 0 \\ \hline \end{array}$$
This figure clearly satisfies the conditions. Therefore $(2, 2)$ is a good pair.
(1) Let $m = 3$. Find all integers $n \leq 10$ for which $(m, n)$ is a good pair.
(2) Find the number of good pairs $(m, n)$ with both $m$ and $n$ at most $10$. Here pairs that differ only in order, such as $(9, 6)$ and $(6, 9)$, are counted as different.

Compute
$$\frac{7}{12} + \frac{5}{12} \times \frac{7}{11} + \frac{5}{12} \times \frac{4}{11} \times \frac{7}{10} + \frac{5}{12} \times \frac{4}{11} \times \frac{3}{10} \times \frac{7}{9}.$$
In a quadrilateral $ABCD$, $AB = 5$, $BC = 7$, $CD = 6$, and the diagonals $AC$ and $BD$ are perpendicular, meeting inside the quadrilateral. Find $DA$.
Find all rational numbers that can be written as $\dfrac{m}{n}$ with positive integers $m, n$ not exceeding $20$ and that are greater than $\dfrac{5}{7}$ and less than $\dfrac{3}{4}$.

Find one polynomial $f(x, y, z)$ of degree $3$ in $3$ variables with real coefficients satisfying the following conditions.
• $f(x, y, z) + x$ is divisible by $y + z$.
• $f(x, y, z) + y$ is divisible by $z + x$.
• $f(x, y, z) + z$ is divisible by $x + y$.
Here a polynomial $P(x, y, z)$ is divisible by a polynomial $Q(x, y, z)$ if there exists a polynomial $R(x, y, z)$ with $P(x, y, z) = Q(x, y, z)R(x, y, z)$.

There is a $5 \times 5$ grid; in each cell of its upper-left $4 \times 4$ part one of the integers $1, 2, \ldots, 16$ is written so that the numbers written in any $2$ cells are distinct ($\clubsuit$). For each of rows $1$ to $4$, the sum of the $4$ numbers written in that row is written in the empty cell at the right end of that row. Similarly, for each of columns $1$ to $4$, the sum of the $4$ numbers written in that column is written in the empty cell at the bottom of that column. Nothing is written in the lower-right cell. Find the largest integer $m$ satisfying the following condition.
Condition: by writing the numbers suitably at stage ($\clubsuit$), one can arrange that in the $5$th column there are $2$ cells whose written numbers differ by at least $m$, and in the $5$th row there are $2$ cells whose written numbers differ by at least $m$.
In a triangle $ABC$, let $D, E, F$ be the midpoints of $BC, CA, AB$ respectively; then $AD = 3$, $BE = 4$, $CF = 5$. Find the area of $ABC$.

The diagonals $AC$ and $BD$ of a quadrilateral $ABCD$ meet at a point $P$ inside the quadrilateral. If $AC = 2$, $BD = 3$ and $\angle APB = 60^\circ$, find the smallest possible value of $AB + BC + CD + DA$.

$n$ is a $4$-digit positive integer whose tens digit is not $0$; regarding the first $2$ digits and the last $2$ digits of $n$ as $2$-digit integers, the product of these $2$ numbers is a divisor of $n$. Find all such $n$.
(Proof problem: a proof must be written.)

There is a $19 \times 19$ grid. A rectangle all of whose sides lie along the grid lines is called a "good rectangle". Find the smallest integer $n$ satisfying the following condition.
Condition: however $9$ cells are removed, the remaining part can be divided into at most $n$ good rectangles.
(Proof problem: a proof must be written.)

$$877 \times 879 - 121 \times 123.$$

Taro went shopping carrying one each of a $1000$-yen note, a $100$-yen coin, a $10$-yen coin and a $1$-yen coin, bought an item, and used all $4$ of them in payment. How many values are possible for the price of the item?
Here Taro chooses, among the ways of paying in which the money he pays and the change have nothing in common, the way that minimises the number of notes and coins he has after receiving the change.
The change is given with the smallest possible number of notes and coins. The change may also be $0$ yen.

There is a square $ABCD$ with side length $1$. Let $O$ be the circle with diameter $AD$, and take the point $E$ on the side $AB$ so that the line $CE$ is tangent to $O$. Find the area of triangle $CBE$.

A kendo tournament had $6$ participants, and each person fought each of the other $5$ exactly once. Moreover, everyone won a different number of matches. How many combinations of match results are possible? Here draws cannot occur.

How many triples of positive integers $(a, b, c)$ are there such that the least common multiple of $a, b, c$ is $720$? Triples in which the $3$ numbers are in a different order are counted as different.

A junior high school decided to plant tulip bulbs. Everyone plants at least $1$ bulb, and students of the same grade plant the same number of bulbs; then there are $6$ possible numbers less than $100$ for the number of bulbs planted, and the $2$ smallest of them were $52$ and $64$.
Find the possible combinations of the numbers of students in the 1st, 2nd and 3rd grades.

$2008$ boys and $2008$ girls gather for a present exchange. Each boy prepares a bouquet of flowers and each girl a chocolate as a present. Everyone stands in a circle facing inwards, and at each signal everyone simultaneously passes the present they hold to the person on their right. A boy leaves the circle as soon as he receives a chocolate, and a girl leaves the circle as soon as she receives a bouquet.
At most how many signals are needed until everyone has left the circle?
(Proof problem: even though an answer is asked for, it must be proved correct.)

Consider a grid of $3$ rows and $3$ columns made up of $9$ unit squares. The squares are numbered as in the figure below.
$$\begin{array}{|c|c|c|} \hline 1 & 2 & 3 \\ \hline 8 & & 4 \\ \hline 7 & 6 & 5 \\ \hline \end{array}$$
$A, B, C, D$ are points in the interiors (boundaries excluded) of squares $1, 3, 5, 7$ respectively. Let $X$ be the sum of the areas of the common parts of the quadrilateral $ABCD$ with squares $1, 3, 5, 7$, and $Y$ the sum of the areas of the common parts of the quadrilateral $ABCD$ with squares $2, 4, 6, 8$. Prove that $X < Y$.

$m, n$ are positive integers. We want to colour each cell of an $m \times n$ grid red, blue or black so that all of the following conditions hold.
• Every red cell is adjacent to exactly $1$ blue cell and exactly $1$ black cell.
• Every blue cell is adjacent to exactly $1$ black cell and exactly $1$ red cell.
• Every black cell is adjacent to exactly $1$ red cell and exactly $1$ blue cell.
Here $2$ distinct cells are adjacent if they share a side. Answer the following.
(1) For $m = 3$, $n = 4$, find one colouring satisfying the above conditions. (The answer alone suffices.)
(2) Find all pairs $(m, n)$ for which a colouring satisfying the above conditions is possible. (Proof problem.)

There are $2$ three-digit positive integers, each of which has units digit and tens digit both equal to $9$. Find all possible values of the thousands digit of the product of these $2$ numbers.

There is a convex pentagon all of whose sides have length $1$, and some $2$ of its diagonals form an angle of $90^\circ$. Find the largest possible area of such a pentagon.

Find the smallest positive integer $n$ for which $14n, 16n, 18n, 20n$ all have the same number of positive divisors.

There is one ball with each integer from $1$ to $9$ written on it, and some of them are chosen. In how many ways can they be chosen so that the following condition holds? Choosing no ball at all also counts as $1$ way.
Condition: by suitably putting some of the chosen balls into a red box and the remaining chosen balls into a blue box, one can arrange that there are no $2$ balls in a box of the same colour whose written numbers differ by $3$ or more.
Find the number of positive integers with at most $2009$ digits that can be written as $a^{2009} + b^{2009}$ with integers $a, b$.

There is a $2$-digit positive integer. Multiplying it by $7$ gave a $3$-digit number. Multiplying that again by $7$ still gave a $3$-digit number. How many integers are possible as the original integer?

There are $4$ spade playing cards with the numbers $1, 2, 3, 4$ written on them, $6$ heart cards with the numbers $1, 2, 3, \ldots, 6$, and $8$ diamond cards with the numbers $1, 2, 3, \ldots, 8$. When $3$ cards in total are chosen, one of each suit, in how many ways can they be chosen so that the sum of the numbers written on the $3$ chosen cards is a multiple of $7$?

There is a balance; on the left pan there is one weight of each of the weights $22, 24, 26, 28$, and on the right pan one weight of each of the weights $23, 25, 27, 29$. The pan on which the total weight of the weights is larger tilts down, and the balance is level when the totals are equal. The following is repeated until the balance is level: remove $1$ weight from the pan that is tilted down at that moment. In how many ways can the weights be removed so that all the weights have been removed when the balance becomes level?

Let $a_1, a_2, \ldots, a_{100}$ be a permutation of $1, 2, \ldots, 100$, and for each integer $n$ between $1$ and $100$ inclusive define the integer $s_n$ by
$$s_n = \begin{cases} 1 & (a_n > n), \\ 0 & (a_n = n), \\ -1 & (a_n < n). \end{cases}$$
How many tuples of integers $(s_1, s_2, \ldots, s_{100})$ are possible?
Here a permutation of $1, 2, \ldots, 100$ is a sequence of length $100$ in which each integer from $1$ to $100$ appears exactly once.

Let $N$ be a positive integer. Find the largest possible value of $N$ for which there exist $2N$ positive integers $a_1, a_2, \ldots, a_N, x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_N$ satisfying all of the following conditions.
• $x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_N$ are all divisors of $9 \cdot 10^{100}$.
• For every integer $i$ with $1 \leq i \leq N - 1$, $x_i \neq x_{i+1}$.
• For every integer $i$ with $1 \leq i \leq N - 1$, $a_{i+1}$ is obtained by appending $x_i$ to the end of $a_i$.
• For every integer $i$ with $1 \leq i \leq N$, $a_i$ is a multiple of $x_i$.
Here, for positive integers $s, t$, the number obtained by appending $t$ to the end of $s$ is the integer obtained by writing the decimal representation of $t$ immediately after the decimal representation of $s$. For example, appending $22$ to the end of $2024$ gives $202422$.
When the positive integers $m, n$ satisfy $m + n = 2025$, find the largest possible value of the greatest common divisor of $m$ and $n$.

Initially there is $1$ box containing $50^{25}$ stones. Consider repeating the following operation.
Take $1$ stone out of every box containing at least $1$ stone. Then prepare a new empty box and put all the stones taken out into it.
When the $50^{25}$-th operation is finished, how many boxes contain at least $1$ stone?

Let $n$ be an integer with $n \geq 5$. On each of $n$ cards one integer is written, and the following holds.

However at least $n - 3$ and at most $n$ cards are chosen, the mean of the integers written on the chosen cards is an integer.

There is a $30 \times 30$ grid, and $30$ of its cells were painted black so that each row and each column contains exactly $1$ black cell, and the top-left corner cell was painted black. Moreover, there did not exist an integer $n \geq 4$ and $n$ distinct cells $W_1, W_2, \ldots, W_n$ satisfying all of the following conditions.
• None of $W_1, W_2, \ldots, W_n$ is painted black.
• For every integer $i$ with $1 \leq i \leq n$, $W_i$ and $W_{i+1}$ are adjacent, sharing a side. Here $W_{n+1}$ means $W_1$.
• For each integer $i$ with $1 \leq i \leq n$, let $C_i$ be the centre of $W_i$; then there is a black cell inside the closed polygonal line obtained by joining $C_1, C_2, \ldots, C_{n-1}, C_n, C_1$ in this order.
How many paintings of the cells are possible? Here paintings that coincide after rotation or reflection are counted as different.

Let $a_1, a_2, \ldots, a_7$ be positive integers. Consider A and B taking a test consisting of $7$ problems numbered $1, 2, \ldots, 7$. For each integer $i$ with $1 \leq i \leq 7$, solving problem $i$ correctly earns $a_i$ points, and not solving it earns $0$ points. Regardless of which problems A and B solved correctly, both of the following conditions held.
• If A solved more problems correctly than B, A's total score is larger than B's total score.
• If A and B solved the same number of problems correctly, there is a problem solved correctly by exactly one of A and B, and the one with the largest number among such problems was solved correctly by A, then A's total score is larger than B's total score.
Find the smallest possible value of $a_7$.

$1003$ Go players took part in a Go tournament. In this tournament every player played each of the other $1002$ players exactly once; the games against $1000$ of them were decided by a win or a loss, and the games against the remaining $2$ were draws.
A group of at least $3$ players is called a good group if the following holds.
By arranging all the players of the group in a circle facing inwards in a suitable order, one can make every player beat the player immediately to their right.
Let $m$ be the smallest possible number of good groups when every player belongs to at least $1$ good group. Let $N$ be the total number of combinations of game results for which every player belongs to at least $1$ good group and there are exactly $m$ good groups; find the value of $\dfrac{N}{1003!}$.
Here $1003! = 1 \times 2 \times \cdots \times 1003$.

How many $2026$-digit positive integers, each of whose digits is $1$, $2$ or $3$, satisfy the following for every integer $i$ with $1 \leq i \leq 2025$?
• If $i$ is even, the $(i+1)$-th digit from the right is one of the digits among $1, 2, 3$ that occur most often in the last $i$ digits.
• If $i$ is odd, the $(i+1)$-th digit from the right is one of the digits among $1, 2, 3$ that occur least often in the last $i$ digits.

A positive integer whose digit average is not an integer is called an odd-average number. For example, $\dfrac{2+0+2+6}{4} = \dfrac{5}{2}$ is not an integer, so $2026$ is an odd-average number. Find the smallest positive integer $n$ for which $n, n+1, \ldots, n+7$ are all odd-average numbers.
